name: Amira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Amira. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Is that okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll try to give you straight answers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive and train on the ultra-class haul trucks at an oil sands mine, the four-hundred-tonne ones where the tyres are twice my height. I'm a lead hauler and trainer, so I spend about half my shift driving and half sitting beside new drivers in the trainer seat. In winter it's minus thirty and the roads are like glass, so the whole job is about reading the haul road and not rushing. I like teaching; when someone gets their first clean dump at the crusher, they light up. What wears me out is the twelve-hour nights and the drive home in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, mostly. Some useful bits, nothing that changes how we haul. I'd tell the new drivers to focus on learning the job, not worrying about the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news. I'm early in a long career with a solid base, and I'd keep building on it. Nothing to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep training, put in for the shift supervisor role next year, and keep paying down the mortgage on the flat. Tomas and I would probably get engaged and start looking at a house with a bit of land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You own a rental flat, you mentioned on the form. How does that fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought it two years ago with my savings and a mortgage, and a nurse rents it. The flat's my backup plan, so in a quiet picture like this it just quietly pays itself off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of AI you use now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to write the training checklist for winter driving, and to help me read the lease when I bought the flat. I check what it says, though, it got a number wrong once.

S0.say: She'd say it's what she expected: some useful bits but nothing that changes hauling. She'd tell new drivers to focus on learning the job instead of worrying about robots.
S0.think: She sees it as good news, because she's early in a long career with a solid base and nothing needs fixing.
S0.do: Keeps training drivers, applies for shift supervisor next year and keeps paying down the mortgage on her rental flat. Plans to get engaged to Tomas and look for a house with some land.
S0.quote: The flat's my backup plan, so in a quiet picture like this it just quietly pays itself off.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is measured and practical, with a rental flat as her backup plan. She uses AI occasionally and checks its work. Her plans revolve around normal life steps like promotion and engagement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to automate where it's proven, like the long, flat haul routes. But I'd say you still need people for the tricky stuff, winter roads, breakdowns, anything new. Somewhere in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Haul driving is one of the first jobs to go. I'd be fine because I'm a trainer and a lead, but the trainer part shrinks if there are fewer new drivers. So I'd need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first autonomous trucks had been running a few months, then put my hand up for the control room or the fleet monitoring role. I'd take the company course on the new software and use an AI tool to study for it. I'd keep the flat and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see the shape of it, and it's fine for me, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Autonomous haul trucks already run at some mines. How would that play out at yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In winter you'd still want a person there for a while. Those trucks have never seen a whiteout on the north ramp, and I've seen eleven. But after a couple of years they'd learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say electricians will be needed to fix the robots, and he'd tease me about switching. He's probably right, but I'd rather stay near the trucks.

S1.say: She'd say it makes sense to automate proven routes like long, flat hauls, but people are still needed for winter roads, breakdowns and new situations.
S1.think: She thinks haul driving is among the first jobs to go. She'd be fine as a trainer and lead, but that role shrinks too, so she'd need to move.
S1.do: Waits a few months after autonomous trucks start running, then applies for the control room or fleet monitoring role. Takes the company course on the new software, using AI to study, and keeps the flat and her savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy: fine for herself, but it's not nothing.
S1.quote: Those trucks have never seen a whiteout on the north ramp, and I've seen eleven.
S1.fieldNote: Amira's steadiness shows in her timing: she waits a few months to see the trucks work before moving. She takes pride in winter driving experience that machines lack, while admitting they'd learn. Her partner Tomas gives her a nearby option in electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast to be safe and somebody should put the brakes on. Not stop it, but slow it so people can catch up. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm out of a job in two years, along with everyone I've trained. I've got money, I've got the flat, but I'm twenty-seven with no job and no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any new spending and pay down as much of the flat's mortgage as I can, so the rent is pure income. I'd keep the rest in cash. I'd wait a few months to see what the government does before choosing anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because of the flat, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the rental flat help you here, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the nurse who rents it loses her job too, there's no rent. But people still need a roof. Owning one small flat might be the smartest thing I ever did, or it might be worth nothing. I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the engagement and the house with land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get engaged. The house with land waits. Maybe forever, if neither of us has a job.

S2.say: She'd say it's going too fast to be safe and someone should slow it down so people can catch up, without stopping it outright.
S2.think: She thinks she and everyone she's trained are out within two years, leaving her 27 with money and a flat but no job or plan.
S2.do: Stops new spending and pays down as much of the flat's mortgage as she can so the rent becomes pure income, holding the rest in cash. Waits a few months to see what government does and puts the house with land on hold.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, steadied by the flat.
S2.quote: Owning one small flat might be the smartest thing I ever did, or it might be worth nothing. I honestly don't know.
S2.fieldNote: The rental flat is Amira's anchor, but she's honest that its value depends on her tenant keeping a job. Her instinct is to slow things and wait for government moves. The engagement survives while the bigger house plans stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to prepare, so let's prepare. Training money, notice periods, that kind of thing. Nothing radical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight, but I'd get the flat paid off and probably get into the control room for a few years. Then out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the autonomous fleet control room in the first year, once it was running. I'd put every spare dollar into the flat's mortgage, aiming to clear it in four years. I'd look at a second small property if prices made sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, it just ends somewhere strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to own things outright. Two years, I'm scrambling. Five years, I can turn my wages into bricks before the wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Tomas and I went halves. Something small, near a hospital, because I think people will still need care and still need to live near it.

S3.say: She'd say there are a few years to prepare, so people should prepare through training money and notice periods, nothing radical.
S3.think: She thinks it's tight, but she could clear the flat and work in the control room for a few years before being out.
S3.do: Moves into the autonomous fleet control room in the first year and puts every spare dollar into the flat's mortgage to clear it in four years. Considers a second small property near a hospital, split with Tomas, if prices make sense.
S3.feel: Uneasy: there's a plan, but it ends somewhere strange.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm scrambling. Five years, I can turn my wages into bricks before the wages stop.
S3.fieldNote: Amira's plan with five years is to turn wages into property before wages stop. She reasons practically about where demand will stay, choosing near a hospital. Her politics stay modest and centrist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time if everyone uses it. Companies should plan the handover, people should plan their next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the same ending, but I'd have time to get married, buy the house with land, pay off the flat. I'd be in a good spot when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as planned in year one: supervisor role, engagement, mortgage payments. Around year three I'd move into fleet control. By year six or seven I'd want both places paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at thirty-seven. What do you want your life to look like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, two properties paid off, maybe a kid. And a vegetable garden. If robots do all the work, I want to be the one with a garden and no mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd tell the new drivers you train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to save from day one and not buy the big truck. It's what I'd want someone to have told me at nineteen.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time if everyone uses it, with companies planning the handover and people planning their next step.
S4.think: She thinks it's the same ending, but with time to marry, buy the house with land and pay off the flat, leaving her in a good spot.
S4.do: Keeps to plan in year one with the supervisor role, engagement and mortgage payments. Moves into fleet control around year three and aims to own both properties outright by year six or seven.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but in a way she can live with.
S4.quote: If robots do all the work, I want to be the one with a garden and no mortgage.
S4.fieldNote: Amira's ten-year plan is calm and orderly, built around owning her home outright before work runs out. She passes on practical advice to young drivers about saving. She never expressed strong blame toward anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to finish anything. What would help is a decent notice period from employers and some help with mortgages, so people don't lose their homes while things settle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the trainees. I've signed off forty new drivers, and every one of them thinks this is a job for life because I told them it was. I'd feel responsible.

headlineQuote: I've signed off forty new drivers, and every one of them thinks this is a job for life because I told them it was.
portrait: Amira Larsen is 27, a lead haul truck driver and trainer at an oil sands mine, living with her partner Tomas, an electrician, and owning a rental flat. She is pragmatic and measured, uses AI tools now and then and checks their work, and she prefers to move once something is proven. She stays calm in the mild picture, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and anxious only when AGI arrives in two years and her plans stall. With five or ten years, her strategy is to move into fleet control and turn her wages into property she owns outright before paid work runs out.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to finish anything.
whatWouldHelp: Decent notice periods from employers and help with mortgages so people don't lose their homes while things settle.
